extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, benefit-granting agencies, state/local/tribal governments, and members of the public providing comments on the DHS public charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and definitions DHS proposes to use to determine whether an alien is "likely at any time to become a public charge," including household composition, factors to weigh under the totality of the circumstances, treatment of affidavits of support, and how benefit receipt is considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "likely at any time to become a public charge"
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to define “likely at any time to become a public charge” to mean likely at any time in the future to receive one or more public benefits, as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b), based on the totality of the alien’s circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this proposed definition, DHS would find an alien inadmissible as a public charge if DHS finds the alien is likely at any time in the future to receive one or more public benefits in an amount or for a duration exceeding the thresholds described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between current receipt and likelihood to become a public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to distinguish between an alien who is a public charge based on current receipt of public benefits and an alien who is likely to become a public charge at any time in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current receipt of public benefits by itself does not automatically mean the alien is likely to receive public benefits in the future; an alien receiving benefits at time of application is not necessarily inadmissible. Receiving public benefits by itself does not establish that an alien is likely to become a public charge; the determination must be predictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective determination based on totality of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes codifying the public charge inadmissibility determination as a prospective determination based on the totality of an alien’s circumstances at the time of adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review is predictive: assess whether the alien is likely at any time in the future to become a public charge. Other than an absent or insufficient required affidavit of support, no single factor or circumstance would determine the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a required affidavit of support
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of a statutorily required affidavit of support under section 213A of the Act conclusively establishes an alien’s inadmissibility on public charge grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family-sponsored immigrants and certain employment-based immigrants are subject to the requirement. An absent or insufficient affidavit is dispositive regardless of other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated factors for totality of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes that the totality of the circumstances standard would include an alien’s age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Government’s discretion, the determination can also account for an affidavit of support filed under section 213A of the Act. DHS would weigh positive and negative considerations across these factors; if negative factors outweigh positive, alien would be found inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household size used in public charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of public charge inadmissibility determinations, DHS proposes to consider the alien’s household size as part of the family status factor and the assets, resources, and financial status factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household size affects calculation of whether household income is at least 125 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG). Number of children (including U.S. citizen children) may count toward household size, but direct receipt of benefits by those children would not factor into the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS proposed definition of household (adult applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the alien is 21 years of age or older, or under 21 and married (thus not a child), the alien’s household would include: the alien; the alien's spouse, if physically residing with the alien; the alien's children physically residing with the alien; other children for whom the alien provides or is required to provide at least 50% financial support (evidenced by orders/agreements); any other individuals (including a spouse not physically residing) to whom the alien provides or is required to provide at least 50% support or who are listed as dependents on the alien's federal tax return; and any individual who provides the alien at least 50% of the alien’s financial support or lists the alien as a dependent on his/her tax return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: a 23-year-old living with two children and parents who provide 53% of her financial support — household size = 5 and their income counted for the 125% FPG test.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS proposed definition of household (child applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the alien is a child as defined in INA section 101(b)(1), the alien’s household would include: the alien; the alien's children physically residing with the alien; other children for whom the alien provides or is required to provide at least 50% support; the alien’s parents/legal guardians or others providing at least 50% support to the alien; the parents’ or guardians’ other children physically residing with the alien; the parents’ or guardians’ other children not residing with the alien for whom the parents/guardians provide at least 50% support; and any other individuals to whom the parents/guardians provide or are required to provide at least 50% support or who are listed as dependents on the parents’/guardians’ federal tax return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a five-year-old living with mother, father, two siblings, and maternal grandparents whom the parents provide 52% support for — DHS would count all those incomes in assessing whether the household meets 125% of FPG.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50 percent financial support threshold for household inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS would adopt the IRS consideration of the amount of support being provided (50 percent) as the threshold for considering an individual part of an alien’s household, regardless of physical residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures individuals the alien supports even without legal obligation. Examples: a younger sibling getting 51% support from the alien is part of the household; an older sibling providing 51% support to the alien would also be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from household
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed household definition would not include persons employed by the household who are living in the home (such as a nanny), or an individual who is renting part of the home from one of the household members, or a landlord, unless such individual otherwise meets the enumerated criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to other program definitions (SNAP, HUD, IRS) and DHS choices
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS reviewed household/family definitions used by other public benefit programs (SNAP, HUD, IRS) but is not adopting SNAP's 'who lives together and purchases/prepares meals together' test and does not precisely track HUD or IRS definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS focuses on individuals for whom the alien (or the alien's parents/guardians) provides at least 50% financial support because such expenditure bears on assets/resources. DHS’s definition would generally capture more people than IRS dependent rules and would include alien dependents IRS would exclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sponsor and affidavit of support in household/income calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The affidavit of support may be considered in the totality of circumstances. The proposed household definition does not automatically include the sponsor and sponsor’s household unless the sponsor provides 50% or more of the alien’s financial support or otherwise meets household criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sponsor is part of the alien’s household and included in the 125% FPG calculation, DHS would count the sponsor’s income once and add it to the alien’s household income. The sponsor’s income is not increased because the sponsor submitted an affidavit of support. Example: sponsor income at 250% of FPG would be added to the alien’s household income and counted as a heavily weighted positive factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting guidance: positive and negative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS’s proposed totality of circumstances standard would involve weighing positive and negative considerations across enumerated factors; if negative factors outweigh positive factors, the alien would be found inadmissible; if positive factors outweigh negative factors, the alien would not be found inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain thresholds constitute strong positive factors (e.g., household income at a high multiple of FPG is 'heavily weighed positive'). No single factor (other than absent/insufficient affidavit when required) is dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past or current receipt of public benefits is insufficient alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving public benefits by itself does not establish that an alien is likely to become a public charge; the statutory public charge determination requires an opinion as to the likelihood of future events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past or current receipt may be considered as one factor but cannot alone sustain a finding of likelihood to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for comment on benefit-granting agencies' procedural modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS requests public comment regarding potential modifications that benefit-granting agencies may make (e.g., advising potential beneficiaries of immigration consequences), including how long it would take and the resources required to make such modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may use this information to determine appropriate effective dates for a final rule and seeks comments from potentially affected state, local, and tribal governments and the public.
